title: The householder's path
hookLine: the Gurus chose family life over renunciation

cards: Back to the circle of yogis, the Siddhas of the Siddh Gosht. These were men who had walked away from everything: wives, children, fields, money, houses. To them, a person tied to a family was tied down.
And here is Guru Nanak in front of them, a man tradition remembers with a wife and sons, who would go home and farm.
In the janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, the yogis invite him to join them, to take up their dress and their road. The door to the renouncer's life is wide open. Which way does he turn?

teach.b: Grihasth means the householder's life: marriage, children, work, a kitchen, bills, neighbors. To the yogis, the high road to God meant leaving all that behind. In the Siddh Gosht itself, Guru Nanak answers with a picture.

teach.h: THE LOTUS STAYS IN THE POND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: as the lotus stays untouched in the water, and the duck swims on the stream without its feathers getting soaked, so a person can live in the world with attention on the Word.
The lotus doesn't leave the pond. It just isn't drowned by it.

In Raag Suhi he says it another way, in paraphrase: in the midst of the soot, stay spotless. The soot is everyday life, the smoke of the kitchen and the market. The teaching isn't to run from the smoke.
It's to stay clean inside it. And the life he chose?
Tradition says Guru Nanak, after his travels, settled at Kartarpur, the farm you met in year one, worked the fields, and lived among family and sangat.
Tradition remembers the Gurus after him living in the world too, not in caves.
So Sikh teaching sets no monk's life above the householder's: holiness is meant to happen at a kitchen table, in a marriage, while raising children. That isn't the easy road. A cave has no toddlers.
This week walked the same road: the mind made a friend, attention, the Word as Guru, book and people, two swords, the shoe counter, and now the home.

how: Sikh teaching honors the householder's path, marrying, working and raising a family in the world, in the pattern tradition remembers from Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur.

o: a vow to leave home and live as a wandering monk
the householder's life of family and work, as a path
a blessing said over a new house before moving in

games.q: the householder's path: tap the pairs.
p: untouched, yet still in the water

s: Guru Nanak teaches that a holy life means leaving family behind
he answers the yogis with the lotus: live in the world, untouched by it.
tradition says Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur and worked the fields
after his travels, among family and sangat.
Sikh teaching ranks leaving home above family life
it sets no monk's life above the householder's; holiness is meant to happen at home.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and the yogis invite you to take up their dress and leave home behind for good. what do you do?
o: accept, and leave family and fields forever.
answer with the lotus, and go home to live in the world.
stay with them for a while, then decide.
games.why: in the Siddh Gosht he answers with the lotus, and tradition says he settled at Kartarpur to farm among family and sangat.

practice: Bring to mind the people you share a home with, or the people you'd call home if you live alone, and see each face.

For each, ask what small thing would make their day lighter, a meal, a call, a chore taken off their list, and hold them as you breathe, the way a lotus holds still on moving water. If you pray, hold them with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Grihasth. The householder's life of family, work and home, which the Gurus lived as a path to the One. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: holiness at home. The lotus stays right there in the pond. That's the week.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi tradition (Guru Nanak with the Siddhas; Kartarpur)
